pr_body:
This commit checksums that backup manifest when it is written. This
helps detect issues such as random bitflips of the manifest data.

When writing a backup manifest, it will also write the checksum of that
file to a file with a "-CHECKSUM" suffix appended to the manifest file
name. The checksum is keyed on the encryption key if the backup is
encrypted. When reading manifests, we check for the '...-CHECKSUM' file,
and if one is present, we compare the checksums. If there isn't one
present, we will continue as we did before. This allows backwards
compatibility with old backups.

I opted for writing the checksum to a new file rather than appending it the
bits to the MANIFEST file just because it was simpler to handle the case
where the checksum didn't exist. Otherwise maintaining 2 versions of the
bytes that we pass through the decompression and optionally attempt to
decrypt was a bit cumbersome.

Fixes #52061.

Release note: None
pr_comments: This change is [](https://reviewable.io/reviews/cockroachdb/cockroach/53292)

Opted to start off with an implementation that writes the checksum to a separate file due to the reason I outlined in the PR description. Don't feel super strongly about it though and am happy to change it to append the bits to the manifest file if that's what others prefer.
Also to note, that this change is intended to detect bitflips before compressing/encrypting. If we wanted to check for bit flips in the file, a SHA-256 hash of the contents would have sufficed.

So upside of checksumming `descBuf` before compressing or encrypting it is that we'll end-to-end testing that we've arrived back at exactly same _proto_ bytes before we decode them. Downside is if we did get an on-disk/wire bit flip or short read or whatever, we still try to decrypt it (which would fail because gcm has an hmac but would be indistinguishable from bad encryption params I believe) and decompress it (which might fail with a cryptic error). If we checksum'ed the bytes we actually wrote to the file -- after compression/encryption, we could be sure we could provide very specific error messages for file corruption (and bad checksum during decrypt would conclusively mean bad enc keys). I could go either way on this.

Agreed -- I was torn on which to focus on. I opted to focus on ensuring that the proto bytes remained the same since bit flips on disk would likely be caught be compression or encryption first. That being said, it's fairly easy to switch which one we want (#53298).

issue_context.title: backupccl: checksum the backup manifest
issue_context.body: The backup manifest stores a considerable amount of metadata, as well as the checksums for the SSTs that are backed up. A bitflip in the manifest would be pretty hard to catch, so we should checksum it.

review_comments: simply mixing the key in to the hash would cause a checksum mismatch if we use the wrong key which could be misleading. If we wanted to checksum the raw bytes, I'd probably actually just encrypt them like the other files.  (but i think i like #53298 better anyway)
